items.description_text: The training aims to develop participants’ practical skills in using films and short films as tools for non-formal youth education and to teach them how to create learning spaces where young people can reflect, express themselves, develop empathy and learn through dialogue. During the course, participants will explore how films and short films can be used in youth work with groups of different levels, interests and needs. They will learn how to select films and scenes according to the objectives of a particular activity, the age and interests of young people, and their diverse needs. Participants will explore practical methods for facilitating discussions and reflection before, during and after a screening, connecting what young people watch with their own experiences and wider social issues. The course will also focus on creating safe spaces for discussing sensitive topics and on adapting screenings, discussions and creative tasks so that young people with different abilities and needs can participate fully. Participants will also learn how to design and test their own film-based activities for youth groups and explore how to create and develop youth film clubs as spaces for shared viewing, dialogue, reflection and interaction. The course provides an opportunity to explore tools of non-formal education, the Erasmus+ programme and international cooperation in youth work. The training is designed as a practical learning process that connects the use of film with concrete methods of non-formal education and approaches that participants can apply in their youth work. Objectives of the training: The main objective of the training is to develop participants’ competencies in using films and methods of non-formal education to create accessible and inclusive learning spaces where young people can reflect, express themselves, develop empathy and learn through dialogue. items.description_text: The Edge Within is an Erasmus+ Training Course for youth workers, trainers, facilitators, educators, community leaders and others actively involved — professionally or voluntarily — in youth work and non-formal learning. Many of us support young people in navigating change, uncertainty, relationships and questions of identity — while meeting similar edges within ourselves. The Edge Within is an invitation to turn some of that attention inward. For one week, 25 participants from Czechia, Latvia, Romania, Italy and Estonia will step away from their everyday routines and gather at an old Scout base surrounded by forests in Nejdek, Czech Republic. Together, we will explore the “edges” within ourselves: our patterns, reactions, boundaries, strengths and the places where we meet uncertainty, discomfort or the not-yet-known. And we will ask how greater awareness of these processes can influence the way we listen, facilitate, hold space and accompany young people. The training combines personal exploration with professional reflection. Through experiential and non-formal learning, nature-based and embodied practices, storytelling, creative expression, movement, reflection, peer learning and community living, participants will first experience the methods themselves — and then explore how they can be meaningfully and ethically adapted to their own youth work. We are looking for people who are curious, open to reflection and willing to participate fully in an experiential learning process. You do not need to be an experienced trainer or have previous experience with nature-based approaches. The setting itself will be part of the journey. We will live simply and closely together, spend meaningful time outdoors and experience November in the Czech countryside as it comes. items.description_text: What if conflict wasn’t a problem to solve, but a language to understand? This project invites you to decode the hidden messages within tension and disagreement, finding paths that lead not just to resolution, but to transformation. By engaging with the roots of conflict and exploring its role in our lives and communities, we’ll explore how it can be a catalyst for creativity, growth, and resilience. This isn’t about avoiding difficulty, it’s about diving into it and reimagining the possibilities on the other side. In a world marked by growing complexity, the need for conflict transformation has never been more urgent. This project invites participants to take a step back, return to the fundamentals, and rediscover the power of dialogue and understanding. Are you ready to shape a new narrative? Aim: To equip 25 youth workers, youth leaders and activists with tools to transform conflicts into opportunities for dialogue and growth, fostering collaboration and building inclusive communities capable of addressing challenges. Objectives - To gain a better understanding of the concepts of Peace, diverse forms of violence, conflict, non-violence and culture of peace. - To understand the importance of nonviolent conflict transformation, the variety of strategies to approach conflict and its links to the context of human rights. - To empower participants to participate and build healthy and peaceful communities and interpersonal relations. - To develop skills in emotional literacy and non-violent communication. - To map and analyse the conflicts affecting the participants in their local context. - To facilitate the process of designing at least 6 follow-up activities aiming to transform local conflicts by using conflict transformation tools. - To create a recommendations document including the framework of competencies for youth leaders to build sustainable communities and teams. Throughout the course, we will ask a central question: Where does AI add real educational value—and where does it not? The course also creates space for an open discussion of ethical concerns, data protection and GDPR, bias, authenticity, over-reliance on technology and the digital divide. Participants will put their learning into practice by building a learning programme step by step with the support of AI, from objectives and activities through to evaluation. items.summary: The webinars explore youth well-being through Body, Mind, Emotions and Connection, combining practical tools, experiential activities and approaches such as Nonviolent Communication, embodiment, mindfulness and creative methods.
items.participants_countries: Erasmus+ Youth Programme countries , Other countries in the world , Partner Countries Neighbouring the EU
items.description_text: Wellness Navigators Webinar Series Wellness Navigators is a series of six free online webinars created for youth workers, educators, trainers, facilitators, and anyone interested in supporting the emotional and social well-being of young people. Running from September 2026 to February 2027, the series explores practical approaches to well-being through the four dimensions of the Wellness Compass: Body, Mind, Emotions, and Connection. Each webinar combines accessible theory with practical tools, reflection, and experiential activities that can be used both for personal development and in educational work with young people. Topics include emotional awareness and regulation, connection and empathy, body-based practices, play and joy, and everyday strategies for strengthening resilience and well-being. The webinars are part of the Wellness Navigators Erasmus+ project, which develops practical educational resources to help young people better recognise their needs, understand their emotional and bodily signals, build healthier relationships, and navigate everyday challenges with greater awareness and choice. What to expect Participants will: discover practical tools for supporting youth well-being; explore the connection between body, thoughts, emotions, and relationships; learn experiential activities that can be adapted to youth work and non-formal education; gain inspiration from approaches such as Nonviolent Communication, embodiment, mindfulness, creative methods, and emotional education; receive access to webinar recordings and additional project resources. The webinars are free of charge and open to an international audience. Participants can register once for the whole six-part series and receive information and access links before each session. The webinar series accompanies the development of the Wellness Navigators toolkit and card deck, offering an opportunity to explore some of the ideas and practices behind the resources in greater depth. items.summary: A hands-on training course for people working with young people, exploring attention, AI and digital habits, and how to practise intentional, present youth work in a hyperconnected world.

items.description_text: Context In the first year of our accreditation, "The Outdoor Youth Work" taught us to use outdoor spaces for non-formal learning. Even outside, we met the same obstacle: attention. In discussions with partners during 2026, youth workers named three difficulties: agreeing on phone use without conflict, bringing a distracted group back to an activity, and responding when young people rely on AI for advice. In the wider context, problematic social media use among adolescents rose from 7% (2018) to 11% (2022) across 44 countries (WHO/HBSC, 2024), and 63.8% of 16-24-year-olds in the EU used generative AI tools in 2025 (Eurostat, 2026). AI gives rapid responses. It can support learning, and it may also encourage distraction, reliance on quick answers or less independent thinking. These effects differ between people and tasks, so youth workers need to observe them in themselves first. The outdoors is our deliberate low-tech contrast: away from notifications and feeds, participants can notice their own habits. Goal To enable youth workers to understand how using AI affects their own attention, critical thinking, confidence and decision-making, and to facilitate activities that help young people stay attentive and make intentional choices about technology. Objectives O1. To increase the self-awareness of 20 youth workers (volunteers, aspiring and active practitioners) regarding how AI use affects their own attention, critical thinking, confidence and decision-making, so that each can distinguish situations where AI supports learning from those where it hinders it. O2. To strengthen the competence of the 20 youth workers to facilitate inclusive, well-debriefed activities on attention and to make reasoned decisions on whether AI serves an activity's learning purpose. items.description_text: Main aim To improve our educational impacts through experiencing a non-formal educational (NFE) process Why this Training Course? Young people are navigating uncertainty, rapid social change, digital pressure, polarization and declining motivation in education, while youth workers are expected to respond with empathy, stability and inclusive support to these situations. Alongside emotional distress, many youth workers report growing levels of low motivation, disengagement, apathy and lack of initiative among young people, which directly affects participation in learning, community life and democratic processes. However, the emotional demands placed on youth workers are rising faster than the availability of structured training that equips them to manage emotions, both their own and those of the young people they work with, in a healthy, professional and sustainable way. In this context, emotional intelligence is no longer an optional “soft skill,” but a core competence for high-quality youth work, wellbeing promotion, motivation, participation and democratic engagement. "E-motion: A Practical Guide to Emotional Intelligence in Youth Work" training course is designed to respond to this gap by strengthening youth workers’ emotional intelligence as a key professional competence. While youth work is fundamentally based on human relationships, emotional intelligence competences such as self-awareness, emotional regulation, empathy, motivation and constructive communication are often insufficiently addressed within existing non-formal education training pathways. Youth workers frequently lack practical tools to respond to emotional withdrawal, low self-confidence, reduced intrinsic motivation and fear of failure, especially among young people with fewer opportunities. items.description_text: Summary of the Project Learn more about us on IG What does democracy truly mean beyond casting a vote every four years? Is participation limited to the ballot box, or is it a daily practice of shaping public affairs with awareness, care, and intention? This project, Democracy Lab, invites youth workers, leaders, and active young people to explore democratic participation not merely as an institutional duty, but as a lived experience of community building, solidarity, and empathy. Set against the backdrop of the Spanish general elections happening concurrently during the training, we will use this unique timing to explore and deconstruct political culture, party systems, and electoral laws in Spain, comparing them critically with the realities and systems of other European countries. Together, we will reflect on how meaningful participation intersects with human rights and collective responsibility. Aim To empower 25 youth workers and youth leaders to foster meaningful and democratic participation in their local communities, expanding their understanding of democratic processes, human rights, and solidarity-based practices. Objectives To explore the conceptual framework of human rights, political participation, and community building. To analyze and compare political cultures, party systems, and electoral laws in Spain (coinciding with the general elections) with particularities of participating countries. items.description_text: About the Training Course What if creating a truly inclusive environment was less about complex theories and more about practical, everyday actions? Action for Inclusion is a training course focused on providing you with new strategies and resources to improve inclusiveness in youth work. Throughout the week, participants will explore the different variables that can become hidden barriers to participation and, most importantly, discover how to dismantle them. The main goal is not just to talk about diversity. It is to discover how to actively build safe spaces, support mental health and manage sensitive realities within our communities. The training will give participants the opportunity to practice these strategies and develop the confidence to address discrimination and incorporate inclusive tools directly into their own educational and youth work activities. What will you get from the Training? You will have the chance to: - Deepen your understanding of what really means to be inclusive in our daily lives. - Acquire practical resources to design and implement inclusive strategies in your working environment. - Create safe spaces with a transversal perspective of the people you’re working with. - Manage sensitive topics confidently within your organisations and communities. - Develop the trust and competences needed to identify and address the discrimination towards different groups. - Face the challenges related with mental health and other obstacles against inclusion in your youth work practices. - Create new international connections and opportunities for cooperation Two experienced facilitators The training will be delivered by Víctor Paterna and Santiago Gallego, two experienced trainers and workers from the NGO sector. Through intensive days filled with practical methods, dynamic activities, and peer exchange, you will explore group dynamics, practice debriefing, and discover how to handle challenging moments in a group. Along the way, we will dive into modern digital tools and AI to support your preparation and project workflow in an effective yet responsible way. You will also get hands-on experience by designing and delivering your own workshop live, receiving feedback from peers and trainers. items.description_text: The European Network of Refugee, Migrant and Stateless Changemakers (ENRMSC) invites youth workers, youth leaders, trainers, community practitioners and other professionals working in non-formal learning and youth work to join the first session of Equal Ground, a quarterly ENRMSC dialogue series exploring meaningful participation, access to opportunities and accountability. About the session A seat at the table means little if the decisions are already made. Equal Ground Q1: Meaningful Participation — Beyond the Seat at the Table explores what meaningful participation looks like when refugees, migrants, stateless people and other communities are not simply invited into conversations, but have genuine opportunities to influence decisions, policies and actions. The session will examine the difference between being present and participating meaningfully. Who gets invited to the table? Who gets heard? Who gets to influence what happens next? Through a participatory, community-centred dialogue, participants will explore barriers to meaningful participation and consider how youth workers, organisations and institutions can create more effective pathways for people with lived experience to contribute to decision-making. What will participants explore? items.description_text: TC WINTER 27 – Adventure and Experiential Learning for Personal Growth & Wellbeing is an immersive training course for youth workers, trainers, facilitators and educators interested in exploring how adventure, nature and experiential learning can support personal development and wellbeing. The training is built around a simple principle: experience becomes learning when we create the space to reflect on it, give it meaning and connect it with our everyday life and professional practice. Throughout the programme, participants will be actively involved in outdoor activities, individual and group challenges, reflective practices and facilitated learning processes. The experiences will engage the physical, emotional, cognitive and relational dimensions of learning, inviting participants not only to learn new methods, but also to observe themselves within the learning process. The course will explore how adventure and experiential learning can help people develop greater self-awareness, confidence, resilience, emotional regulation, connection with others and a stronger sense of personal wellbeing. Participants will have the opportunity to: experience adventure and outdoor experiential learning first-hand; explore the relationship between experience, reflection and personal growth; develop greater awareness of their own resources, limits and learning patterns; understand how nature and adventure can contribute to wellbeing and meaningful learning; explore facilitation and reflective practices that help transform an experience into learning; exchange practices and perspectives with youth workers and educators from different European contexts; reflect on how these approaches can be transferred into their own work with young people. The methodology will be highly experiential and participatory. items.summary: Life in It is a two-part Erasmus+ media training for youth workers and educators, combining practical filmmaking, storytelling and short-form video in Germany and Greece, with local practice between the two phases.
items.participants_countries: Czech Republic, Germany, Greece, Italy, Latvia, Poland, Romania, Slovak Republic

items.accommodation_food_text: All accommodation and food costs will be covered by the programme.

items.description_text: Life in It is a two-part Erasmus+ media training for people active in youth work and non-formal learning, including youth workers, trainers, educators, volunteers, project coordinators and people involved in their organisation’s communication. No previous filmmaking experience is required; the focus is on learning through practice, collaboration and experimentation. The learning journey starts with online preparation and continues with Frame One in Germany (13–19 December 2026), where participants explore practical filmmaking, storytelling and media tools by working in international crews and creating content in real local contexts. Between the two international phases, participants bring the learning into their own organisation or community, including a small focus group with young people and further local practice. The journey continues with Frame Two at Hopeland, Greece (22–29 September 2027), where participants explore how the same storytelling foundations can be adapted to shorter, vertical video and social media formats. The methodology is strongly based on non-formal education and learning by doing: short inputs, practical assignments, teamwork, feedback, reflection and creative decision-making are at the centre of the programme. Life in It is designed as one learning journey rather than two separate trainings, with online preparation, two residential phases, local practice and follow-up. Priority is given to applicants who can take part in the complete process and use the learning afterwards in their youth work, organisation or local community.

items.summary: A practical training for youth workers to discover circus and theatre as tools for non-formal education, exploring accessible activities that foster creativity, confidence, cooperation and social connection.

items.description_text: This training course introduces youth workers, educators and facilitators to circus and theatre as practical tools for youth work and non-formal education. No previous circus or theatre experience is required. Through hands-on activities, participants will discover the basics of juggling, partner and group acrobatics, clowning and physical theatre, while learning how to adapt these activities into accessible and meaningful workshops for young people. The course is based on circus pedagogy: an educational approach that uses circus not primarily to train performers, but to support personal and social development. Circus activities create opportunities to cooperate, communicate, build trust, take on challenges, be creative and experience success. Participants will explore how these activities can foster young people's confidence, creativity, cooperation, persistence, coordination and social connection. A key focus will be accessibility and inclusion, exploring how circus can be adapted to different ages, physical abilities, levels of experience and backgrounds. Participants will also discover how a group can move from individual games and activities towards creating a short collective performance. They will explore the pedagogical and practical aspects of the creative process, including generating ideas, sharing roles, connecting different disciplines and ensuring that everyone can contribute. By the end of the training, participants will have a practical repertoire of circus and theatre activities and greater confidence in using them in their youth work.

items.description_text: Project Summary: Leveraging ICT and Social Media for Youth Inclusion and Participation Aim of the Project: The project is designed to equip youth workers with digital skills and tools to strengthen civic participation and engage young people through Information and Communication Technology (ICT). A core aim is to promote civic engagement through digital tools. Objectives: Strengthen Digital Competencies: Provide practical training in ICT, social media engagement, and digital content creation. Youth workers will be trained to guide young people in critical media analysis, recognizing misinformation, and using digital platforms for youth activism and community participation. Ensure Inclusion and Equal Access: Develop strategies to engage marginalized and disadvantaged young people who face barriers to digital participation. Encourage Innovation: Introduce interactive, gamified, and blended learning approaches to make digital engagement more dynamic and adaptive. Strengthen Transnational Cooperation: Establish a European Digital Youth Work Network for collaboration and knowledge exchange, and develop a Digital Civic Engagement Toolkit with practical resources. Outcome: The project aims to significantly enhance the digital skills of youth workers and strengthen youth engagement through the use of digital tools for non-formal education and social participation. It seeks to expand civic participation through youth-led activism and make digital youth work more accessible and inclusive for young people from diverse and disadvantaged backgrounds. The project's sustainability will be ensured through the creation of a European-wide network of digital youth workers and an open-access toolkit, ensuring that the methodologies remain relevant and scalable.

items.description_text: The ENRMSC European Dialogue & Capacity-Building Forum 2027 will take place in Warsaw, Poland, in April 2027. The forum will bring together young refugees, migrants and stateless changemakers, youth workers, youth leaders, researchers, academics, civil society organisations, public institutions and other practitioners working with young people. The forum is built around a simple question: How can we move from young people being affected by systems to young people meaningfully shaping knowledge, opportunities, policies and solutions? The programme will explore meaningful participation, access to education and professional opportunities, community leadership, research and evidence, youth engagement, advocacy and collaboration between communities and institutions. Participants will take part in interactive discussions, panel sessions, workshops and facilitated group activities. The programme will combine knowledge exchange with practical capacity-building and opportunities for participants to develop new connections and potential European cooperation. A particular focus will be placed on recognising lived experience as expertise. Young refugees, migrants and stateless people will not only participate as beneficiaries but as contributors, knowledge holders, community leaders and partners in shaping discussions and recommendations. The forum will also connect participants with relevant European opportunities, networks and potential partners, including opportunities related to youth work, education, research, leadership and civic participation. The event is particularly relevant to people working in non-formal learning and youth work who engage with young people from refugee, migrant and stateless backgrounds. The guiding principle of the forum is: “Nothing About Us Without Us.” The forum is currently being developed by the European Network of Refugee, Migrant and Stateless Changemakers (ENRMSC), a refugee-, migrant- and stateless-led European civil society organisation.

items.description_text: Why this programme? Young people increasingly experience the world through digital, visual, interactive and participatory media. At the same time, heritage education can sometimes remain centred on traditional formats: guided tours, exhibitions, historical information and passive observation. This creates an opportunity for youth work. New media can provide alternative entry points into heritage, allowing young people to: explore places and stories through immersive experiences; discover hidden or forgotten narratives; connect personal and community memories with wider European heritage; question dominant interpretations of history; create their own narratives; collaborate across cultures; transform physical spaces into interactive learning environments. The programme therefore does not aim to turn youth trainers into technology specialists. Instead, it aims to help them become creative facilitators who know when, why and how to use technology to create meaningful learning experiences. General aim To strengthen the capacity of youth trainers to use new media and emerging technologies as tools for heritage awareness, intercultural learning, creativity and youth participation. Specific objectives By the end of the training, participants will be able to: Explore contemporary approaches to cultural heritage and heritage awareness. Identify opportunities for using immersive and interactive media in youth work. Experiment with VR, AR, 360° media, projection mapping, interactive installations, digital storytelling and other creative technologies. Design non-formal education activities connecting young people with local, national and European heritage. Use storytelling and participatory methodologies to make heritage more relevant to young people. Encourage young people to question, reinterpret and remix heritage narratives. About this course International youth mobility projects can create powerful opportunities for learning, participation, connection, and personal growth. items.description_text: The project arises from a shared observation among young people, community development professionals, and partner organizations: a growing need to reconnect with the living world, rebuild social bonds, and collectively reflect on current ecological challenges in the face of the climate emergency. It addresses two main needs: Strengthening the skills of facilitators and community leaders so they can design and implement educational projects with strong social and ecological impact. Actively engaging young people in meaningful, concrete, and transformative projects. The project uses the living garden as an educational, sensory, and cooperative tool, helping to recreate connections between humans and ecosystems. These spaces become platforms for social transformation, civic education, and territorial resilience. It is based on active pedagogy that promotes autonomy, local engagement, and the transversal skills required for the ecological transition. The event will take place outdoors and is aimed at educators, activity leaders, and facilitators. In Brittany, 27 participants are expected.
